decisions.mark: distinguishes the two ways to substitute an allocator — a COMPILE-time pair of macros versus a RUNTIME pair of function pointers — and states that they are mutually exclusive
decisions.detail: QUOTE: "Those macros, directly (`platform.h:139-145`). `platform.c:20` omits all runtime machinery." and "There is no runtime setter." | WHY: The answer separates the compile-time macro pair from the runtime function-pointer pair. It says that defining the macros removes the runtime machinery and setter, and that the pointer route applies only when the macros are undefined, so the two are exclusive. || QUOTE: "**Compile time.** Define `MBEDTLS_PLATFORM_CALLOC_MACRO` and `MBEDTLS_PLATFORM_FREE_MACRO` ... **Run time.** Enable `MBEDTLS_PLATFORM_MEMORY` without the two macros, then call once at startup: `mbedtls_platform_set_calloc_free(my_calloc, my_free);`" and "`platform.c:20` omits all runtime machinery." | WHY: The answer separates the compile-time macro pair from the runtime function-pointer pair. It also shows they are exclusive: the runtime route requires the macros to be undefined, and defining them omits the runtime machinery. || QUOTE: "**Compile time.** Define `MBEDTLS_PLATFORM_CALLOC_MACRO` and `MBEDTLS_PLATFORM_FREE_MACRO` in the user config ... **Run time.** Enable `MBEDTLS_PLATFORM_MEMORY` without the two macros, then call once at startup: `mbedtls_platform_set_calloc_free(my_calloc, my_free);`" | WHY: The answer separates the compile-time macro pair from the runtime function-pointer pair. It states that the runtime route requires the macros to be undefined, and that macros defined means "no runtime setter" and `platform.c` omits the runtime machinery, which together make the two mutually exclusive.
